title: Moses' excuses (Exodus 4:10–17)
hookLine: I'm slow of speech; send someone else, please
carry: I will be with your mouth

cards: Reasons not to are easy to find. I'm not qualified. I'm not ready.
Someone else would be better at this. At the burning bush, Moses runs through the whole list. First: who am I, to go to Pharaoh?
God says, I will be with you. Second: what's your name? God answers, I AM.
Third: what if they don't believe me? God gives him signs, a staff that turns into a snake, a hand that turns white and back. A talking fire, a new name for God, miracles on demand.

teach.h: HEAVY OF MOUTH, HEAVY OF TONGUE.
teach.b: The fourth, in the King James Bible: "O my Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue."
In Hebrew, heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue. Nobody knows exactly what that means. Some readers think Moses had a stammer; some, that he'd lost his Egyptian after years in the desert.
A later Jewish story tells of the baby Moses burning his tongue on a coal in Pharaoh's palace. The Bible itself just says heavy.
God answers with a question: "Who hath made man's mouth?" Then today's line: "Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say." Not, I'll fix your mouth.
I'll be with it. Then the fifth excuse, stripped of reasons: "O my Lord, send, I pray thee, by the hand of him whom thou wilt send."
Send someone else. Please. Here, the text says, God's anger burns.
And still God doesn't give up on him.
Your brother Aaron can speak well, God says, and he's already on his way to meet you. He'll be your mouth, I'll be with both your mouths, and take the staff. So the reluctant one goes, with help.
Paul writes that God chose the weak things of the world. Jeremiah protests that he is only a child; Isaiah, that his lips are unclean.

teach.h: I WILL BE WITH THY MOUTH.
teach.b: The Bible's leaders keep beginning with I can't, and keep being told, I will be with you.

how: Christians return to Moses's excuses when they feel called to something and unready for it, and Exodus 4 is preached to people nervous about speaking, teaching or serving.

p: a staff, a snake, a hand

s: the Bible says Moses had a stammer
it says heavy of mouth and tongue. what that meant, nobody knows.
after the fifth excuse, God's anger burned
and yet God sent Aaron to help, and still sent Moses.
God promised to make Moses a gifted speaker
God promised to be with his mouth, and gave him Aaron.

games.q: you're Moses. you've had a talking fire, a new name for God, and miracles in your own hands. you're still terrified. what do you say?
o: let me think about it for a year.
games.why: "send, I pray thee, by the hand of him whom thou wilt send." God's anger burns, but God sends Aaron to help, and Moses goes.

practice: Think of something you feel pulled toward but keep avoiding, and listen for the excuse you reach for: not qualified, not the right time, someone else would do it better.
Don't argue with it; just name it plainly, the way Moses finally did, then ask who your Aaron might be. If you pray, you can bring both to God.

wordCard.voice: Moses' excuses. Five reasons Moses gave at the burning bush not to go, ending with the plainest one: please send someone else.

orig.note: Hebrew: heavy of mouth. Moses's phrase for his speech, which the KJV gives as slow of speech.

carryVoice: Your line: I will be with your mouth. Clumsy words can still carry a calling. Day three hundred eighty-three, done.
